extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or beginning_graduate students of complex analysis; readers learning rigorous theory of branches, winding numbers, Taylor series, argument principle, and residues
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains textbook-level standards, definitions, and computational rules from an appendix on branches of multi-valued functions, winding numbers, Taylor series operations, the argument principle, and the residue theorem. Useful for solving/validating complex-analysis exercises and contour-integral computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch of the logarithm (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of the logarithm as an analytic function on a set U when exp maps an open set one-one onto U; such a determination is called a (single-valued) branch of the logarithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any branch of the logarithm is a partial inverse of the exponential; if g is such a branch then Proposition B.26 gives g'(e^z)=1/e^z and hence g'(z)=1/z for all z in the branch domain. Domains for branches often are C minus a ray from the origin, but need only be regions where exp has a one-to-one inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal branch of logarithm (Log z)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal branch is the determination that uses U = C \ (−∞, 0] onto (−π, π) i.e. Log z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log z is a one-one analytic function from C \ (−∞,0] onto {w : −π < Im w < π}. Frequently used as the canonical branch when defining other multi-valued functions (e.g., z^p) via exp(p Log z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch of nth root (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of z^{1/n} as an analytic function on a set U when z ↦ z^n maps an open set one-one onto U; such a determination is a branch of the nth root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Inverse Function Theorem to z^n (which has complex derivative n z^{n−1} ≠ 0 on C\{0}) to obtain local analytic inverses. Branches differ by multiplication by nth roots of unity; the principal branch corresponds to a standard choice of argument interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative formula for a branch of nth root
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is a branch of the nth root, then g'(w) = g(w)/(n w).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from differentiating the local inverse relation g(z^n)=z and using Proposition B.26. The formula is valid for every branch of the nth root on its domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of z^p via logarithm (branches of z^p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define z^p for real p by z^p = e^{p Log z}; any branch of the logarithm leads to a branch of z^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principal branch of the logarithm when appropriate (principal branch makes (1−z)^p meaningful near 0 for real p). By the same computation as for nth root, any branch of z^p has the expected complex derivative (text gives the corresponding derivative formula in context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical domain conditions for using principal branches (example: arcsine)
rubrics_metrics.description: When expressing inverse trigonometric functions via logarithms and square roots, one must ensure the argument of the logarithm and the choice of square-root branch avoid exceptional cases (e.g., iw ± sqrt{1−w^2} must not lie on negative real axis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text works through arcsin w expressed using logarithms and square roots and checks the exceptional cases (e.g., when iw ± sqrt{1−w^2} is real and ≤ 0) to decide when the principal branches may be used. Excluding such exceptional sets ensures the chosen principal branches yield well-defined analytic values (e.g., values of the square root lie in the open right half-plane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches (formal note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Branch is taken to mean a consistent determination of an analytic function on a region of C that satisfies appropriate properties for that function (formal definition in terms of 'global analytic functions' omitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inverse function-based definition suffices for logarithm and nth root but is inadequate for general z^p; thus adopt a working definition emphasizing consistent analytic determination on a region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding number / index (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a piecewise C^1 closed curve in C not passing through z0, the winding number n(Γ, z0) is the integer (1/2πi) ∮_Γ dζ/(ζ − z0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, the winding number measures how many times Γ winds around z0; it equals the change in argument of ζ−z0 divided by 2π when the argument is chosen continuously along the curve. It is integer-valued by Proposition B.27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral around closed curve is multiple of 2πi (Proposition B.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a piecewise C^1 closed curve Γ not passing through z0, the complex line integral ∮_Γ dζ/(ζ − z0) is a multiple of 2πi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses parametrization and shows exp of integral equals 1, hence integral ∈ 2πi Z. This justifies definition of winding number as integer (1/2πi times the integral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding number constant on components (Proposition B.28)
rubrics_metrics.description: The function z0 ↦ n(Γ, z0) is constant on each connected component of the open complement of image(Γ) in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: n(Γ, z0) is integer-valued and continuous on regions at positive distance from the curve; integer-valued continuous ⇒ constant on components. Useful for topological reasoning about contours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding number zero on unbounded component (Proposition B.29)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a piecewise C^1 closed curve, then n(Γ, z0) = 0 for z0 in the unbounded component of the complement of image(Γ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate integral by bounding |1/(ζ − z0)| ≤ R/|z0|^2 etc. As |z0|→∞ winding number tends to 0 and is constant on unbounded component, so equals 0 there. Frequently used to assert only interior poles contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple winding-number computations / examples
rubrics_metrics.description: If σ traverses Γ k times over the same image then n(σ, z0) = k n(Γ, z0). For a standard circle centered at a, n(C, z0)=1 for points z0 inside C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples connect the analytic definition with intuitive counting of turns; useful for applying Cauchy and residue formulae with simple contours (circles, rectangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy Integral Formula, general disk form (Theorem B.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be analytic in an open disk D, and Γ any piecewise C^1 closed curve in D. If z ∈ D not on image(Γ), then (1/2πi) ∮_Γ f(ζ)/(ζ − z) dζ = n(Γ, z) f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the Cauchy formula to arbitrary closed curves in a disk by introducing the winding number factor. Proof: apply Cauchy Integral Theorem to suitable auxiliary function with removable singularity at z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor series coefficients: practical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Taylor coefficients may be computed from the definition, but often easier methods are used (algebraic manipulations, known expansions like exp, sin, cos, binomial series). For f analytic near 0, coefficients a_k = f^{(k)}(0)/k! and a remainder term [z^{n+1}] analytic with zero of order ≥ n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find coefficients up to z^n, one does not need full series or radius. Use expansions, differential equations satisfied by sums, geometric series tricks, or equate coefficients after polynomial multiplication. Example: expansion of e^z/(z−1) computed up to given order by manipulating geometric series and known expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term differentiation and integration of power series
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex differentiation and integration may be performed term-by-term on power series within their disk of convergence; differentiation reduces powers, integration increases them (opposite effects on coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration in a disk corresponds to line integrals independent of path. Use termwise operations to obtain expansions like log(1/(1−z)) by integrating geometric series termwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of power series (practical coefficient dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(z)=∑ a_n z^n analytic for |z|<r and g(w)=∑ b_n w^n analytic in a disk containing f(|z|<r), then g(f(z)) is analytic for |z|<r and its Taylor coefficients for z^n depend only on b_0,...,b_n and the a_k up to relevant order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution can be tedious unless f(0)=0. In coefficient computations only finitely many b_k contribute to a given coefficient of z^n (b_0,...,b_n). For polynomial inner functions, composition is straightforward (substitute and collect powers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial series and principal-branch caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The binomial series (1−z)^p (p real) is defined using the principal branch of logarithm when appropriate; for |z|<1 and principal Log branch the binomial series converges to (1−z)^p except when z real and ≥1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principal branch of log is used to define (1−z)^p = exp(p Log(1−z)). Theorem B.21 (Taylor's Theorem) guarantees convergence within radius of analyticity; special-case integer p gives entire convergence. Use integration to produce expansions for arcsin via binomial series as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing inverse-function Taylor coefficients (Inverse Function Theorem approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(z)=a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + ... with a_1 ≠ 0, then the inverse function g(w)=∑ b_n w^n exists locally and its coefficients b_n can be solved recursively by equating coefficients in g(f(z))=z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The low-order relations: b_1 a_1 = 1 ⇒ b_1 = 1/a_1; equate higher-order coefficients to obtain linear equations solvable because a_1 ≠ 0. Radius of convergence of g is positive though not readily estimated by this procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-rule for analytic maps of piecewise C^1 curves (Lemma B.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ(t) is piecewise C^1 curve and f analytic on region containing image(Γ), then f∘Γ is piecewise C^1 and d/dt f(Γ(t)) = f'(Γ(t)) Γ'(t) wherever derivative exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-variable chain rule and Cauchy–Riemann equations to reduce to complex derivative form; needed to relate integrals of f'/f to change in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral formula for logarithmic derivative along image curve (Lemma B.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is piecewise C^1 closed curve and f analytic and nonzero on image(Γ), then n(f∘Γ, 0) = (1/2πi) ∮_Γ f'(z)/f(z) dz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parametrize Γ and apply Lemma B.31 to move derivative inside integral. Interprets logarithmic derivative integral as winding number of f∘Γ about 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument Principle, local form (Proposition B.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be meromorphic in a disk U with zeros {a_j} of orders h_j and poles {b_l} of orders k_l. For any piecewise C^1 closed curve Γ in U not passing through zeros/poles, (1/2πi) ∮_Γ f'(z)/f(z) dz = Σ_j h_j n(Γ, a_j) − Σ_l k_l n(Γ, b_l). Consequently n(f∘Γ, 0) equals the same sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only finitely many zeros/poles contribute because outside a small disk they have winding number 0. Proof uses factorization f(z)=Π (z−a_j)^{h_j} (z−b_l)^{−k_l} g(z) with g analytic and nonvanishing, then logarithmic differentiation; the integral of g'/g vanishes by Cauchy. Use this to count zeros/poles inside curves (with multiplicity) when n(Γ, a_j) is 0 or 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perturbation of zeros / local root-count (Proposition B.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a disk and has a zero of order n at z0, then for sufficiently small c the equation f(z) = c has exactly n roots in a small disk about z0 (counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose small circle about z0 avoiding other zeros and critical points; apply Argument Principle to f(z) − c and continuity of winding number to show count is preserved. This yields corollary that nonconstant analytic maps are open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open mapping theorem corollary (Corollary B.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant analytic function carries open sets onto open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Proposition B.34: for any w0 = f(z0) and sufficiently small disk around w0, preimage contains a small disk around z0 mapped surjectively into an open neighborhood of w0 (modulo local multiplicity behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local factorization near a zero (Corollary B.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic near z0, f(z0)=w0 and f has zero of order n at z0, then locally f(z) = ((z−z0)^n) h(z) and equivalently f(z) can be written as a composition of an analytic function with an nth-power map: f(z) = φ(z)^n with φ analytic and nonvanishing adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct h(z) by factoring out (z−z0)^n and taking principal nth root of normalized factor in neighborhood where normalization avoids negative real axis; choose appropriate constant factor for branch of nth root to get analytic φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue at an isolated pole (definition and simple-pole formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a pole at z0, expand f as sum of singular part plus analytic part; the residue Res f(z0) is the coefficient b1 of (z−z0)^{−1} in the Laurent expansion. For a simple pole, Res f(z0) = lim_{z→z0} (z−z0) f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For higher-order poles of order h, Res f(z0) = (1/(h−1)!) lim_{z→z0} d^{h−1}/dz^{h−1} [(z−z0)^h f(z)]. Compute residues by expansion or differentiation formula where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue Theorem (Theorem B.37)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a disk except for isolated poles z_j and Γ is a piecewise C^1 closed curve in the disk not passing through any pole, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_j Res f(z_j) n(Γ, z_j), only finitely many terms nonzero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: subtract singular parts to get analytic remainder whose integral is 0; integrate principal parts to get 2πi times residues times winding numbers. The formula remains valid for essential singularities though residue-computation method differs (Laurent series required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using residues to evaluate real definite integrals (practical contour method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate real integrals (e.g., ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P(x)/Q(x) dx) pick an appropriate contour (real segment + large semicircle in upper/lower half plane) such that contribution from arc vanishes in limit; then integral equals 2πi times sum of residues of integrand's poles inside contour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} 1/(x^2+1) dx computed by enclosing upper-half plane pole at i. Estimate integrals on the large semicircle (|integrand|·arc_length → 0) to justify ignoring arc contribution. Choose contour orientation so interior is on left; winding numbers equal 1 for interior simple poles.
